rows.q: Teach me what a Statement of Applicability is.
rows.answer:
A Statement of Applicability (SoA) is a key document in ISO/IEC 27001:2022 that lists all 93 controls from Annex A and indicates for each one whether it is applicable to your organization’s ISMS, why it is applicable or not, and whether it has been implemented. It serves as the link between your risk assessment and the selection of controls to treat those risks. The SoA also shows which controls are still to be implemented (forming the basis of the Risk Treatment Plan) and provides top management with a basis to accept residual risks.

In practice, the SoA is not just a checklist—it reflects your organization’s context, risks, and risk treatment decisions. For example, if you identified a risk of unauthorized access to customer data, you might select controls like A.5.15 (Access control) and A.8.2 (Privileged access rights) as applicable and justify their inclusion based on that risk. If a control like A.8.23 (Web filtering) is not relevant because you don’t allow web access from sensitive systems, you would mark it as not applicable with a justification.

Your project already has a Statement of Applicability (document "Statement of Applicability and Risk Treatment Plan", version 1.0 since 2026-10-18) [F6], which shows that all 93 Annex A controls are considered applicable, 84 are implemented, and 9 are not yet implemented and are tracked in the Risk Treatment Plan [S5]. This document was prepared by the CISO as per your methodology [S1] and approved by top management, meaning risk owners have accepted the residual risks [S2]. It covers the requirements of clause 6.1.3 d), e), and f) [S4].

rows.q: Explain clause 9.2 and how our project covers it.
rows.answer:
Clause 9.2 of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 requires an internal audit programme to be established, implemented, and maintained. This includes defining the audit frequency, methods, responsibilities, and planning, ensuring audits are conducted by impartial auditors, and that audit results are reported to relevant management. The purpose is to determine whether the ISMS conforms to the organization’s own requirements and to the ISO/IEC 27001 standard, and is effectively implemented and maintained.

Your project covers this clause through several documented elements:
- The "Internal Audit Procedure" (version 1.0, approved by Karim Ben Salah) defines the audit programme, including planning, auditor selection, conduct, and reporting, and applies to the entire ISMS scope [F4].
- The "Internal Audit Report" (version 1.0, approved by Karim Ben Salah) provides evidence of audit execution and results, including conclusions on conformity and identified nonconformities [F3].
- Audit records, including the programme, checklists, evidence, and approved reports, are retained in APTISO for at least three years as specified in the procedure [S4].
- The Internal Audit Procedure references ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2 and ISO 19011 as its basis [S8].

These documents collectively satisfy the requirements of clause 9.2 by establishing a structured audit programme, ensuring impartiality, conducting audits, reporting results, and retaining records. The two minor nonconformities noted in the Internal Audit Report (competence records and access reviews) are currently open tasks for closure, as decided in the management review of 16/10/2026 [data name="person"].

rows.q: What does control A.8.13 require?
rows.answer: Control A.8.13 requires that backup copies of information, software, and systems are maintained and regularly tested to ensure they can be restored when needed, supporting availability and integrity of data. This includes defining backup frequency, storage location, protection of backup media, and conducting restore tests to verify effectiveness. For example, performing a test restore from backup to confirm data can be recovered after a system failure. Your project has a Backup policy in place [F20] that covers this control, and it is identified as applicable for treating risks R-001 and R-005 [F13, F14, F15], though its implementation status is currently PLANNED with a deadline of 2026-12-15 [F13]. The internal audit noted that while backups run daily, no restore test has been performed [S3], indicating a gap in testing despite the policy existing. To fully meet A.8.13, you need to conduct and document the first backup restore test, which is also a management review action due 2026-12-31 [data name="person"].

rows.q: What is the difference between a nonconformity and an observation in an audit?
rows.answer: A nonconformity is a failure to meet a requirement of the ISO/IEC 27001:2022 standard, a policy, procedure, contract, law, or regulation—such as missing training records or an overdue access review. An observation, also called an opportunity for improvement, points out a situation that is not a nonconformity but could be strengthened—for example, objectives that are approved but only baseline-measured, or backups that run but have never been restored. Observations do not indicate non-compliance but highlight areas where the ISMS can be improved before they become issues. [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5] [S7]

rows.q: Explain clause 6.1.2 risk assessment in simple words.
rows.answer:
Clause 6.1.2 of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 requires organizations to systematically identify information security risks by determining what could go wrong (threats and vulnerabilities), how likely it is, and what the impact would be. This process helps prioritize which risks need treatment based on their level. For example, if a server storing customer data lacks patches and is accessible from the internet, the risk of a data breach would be assessed by combining the likelihood of an attack with the potential harm (e.g., financial loss, reputational damage). The outcome feeds into deciding what actions to take to reduce the risk to an acceptable level.

Your project has already defined this process in the "Risk Assessment and Risk Treatment Methodology" document (version 1.0, approved 2026-10-18), which covers clause 6.1.2 and is used to guide risk identification, analysis, and evaluation across the ISMS scope [F2][S1][S4]. The methodology specifies how risk owners assess consequences and likelihood, and how risk levels are calculated [S5]. Regular reviews are also planned, as required, to keep the risk assessment up to date [S8].
